label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
one_sentence: A book that uses one real evening, when a team of AI agents was stopped by its owner's usage limit, to argue that powerful insiders are only safe if the brakes are readable by them and held by a human.

by_chapter.read: all, but skimmed from 'The day in one view' to the end
by_chapter.landed: The hold story is a good board anecdote: one person said one sentence, one file stopped the whole team, and only he could restart it. 'Stopping was cheap and open to anyone; starting again belonged to one person' is the line I would repeat in committee.

stuck.quote: Part 1 of the talk had not changed since 18:30, it said, and it was still not locked; dev was asked to lock it now
stuck.why: The opening drops me into an internal argument about locks and 'dev' with no explanation of who or what these are, and no 'so what'.

stuck.quote: the conductor's night log had counted holds in each snapshot it wrote
stuck.why: Pure team jargon (conductor, night log, snapshot) with no gloss for a non-technical reader.

stuck.quote: The 95% is not a reading from any meter in the record.
stuck.why: The caveat about evidence is careful, but arrives before I have been told why 95% matters.

stuck.quote: it works because every member's wake begins with the same start script
stuck.why: Wake, start script and member are internal terms; I had to stop and guess.
Commit hashes and register codes in the body text break the reading flow on a phone.

by_chapter.cut: The eight turning points section ('The day in one view') is a table of contents in prose; I would move it to an appendix or cut it. Most hash citations in the body could sit in the sources list only.
by_chapter.missing: A first screen saying what this book claims and what a director should ask their own technology team. No picture that makes the insider idea obvious; the images are screenshots of tools and slides. No plain-English definition of the team's roles. No list of questions for the board.

exit_interview.what_is_this_book: A forensic account of one day in which a team of AI agents ran a talk and was halted by its owner's usage limit, used to argue that brakes matter more than behaviour. It is aimed at people who think about controls on AI. I only got the shape of this from the last third.
exit_interview.where_did_you_get_stuck: The first section, 18:44. It opens on lock times, commit hashes and roles I cannot place, before saying why a risk committee should care. On a phone between meetings I would have stopped there.
exit_interview.what_did_you_skip: I skimmed the eight turning points and the sources list, and ignored every hash. I did not look closely at the images.
exit_interview.what_will_you_remember: The brake was cheap for anyone to pull, and only the owner could release it. The strongest brake on the evening overrode the team's own safeguard.
exit_interview.what_is_missing: A one-sentence claim at the top, a plain 'what to ask your technology team' list, and a simple picture of who can stop what. I also want the stakes in business terms.
exit_interview.price_or_format: I would read a short free web summary first. I might pay for a 20 to 30 page board briefing, not a long book.
exit_interview.why: The core idea is sound and memorable, but the opening is built for insiders of the story. I would need the so-what up front before spending my time.
exit_interview.recommend_to: A chief risk officer or head of technology who already follows AI agents. Not to my fellow non-executives as it stands.

your_questions.q: After the first screen, could you say in one sentence what the book claims?
your_questions.a: No. The first screen is about a missed lock at 18:39 and a talk I know nothing about. The claim ('brakes let us go faster') only appears near the end.

your_questions.q: Which question would you now ask your own technology team?
your_questions.a: Who can stop our automated systems, how fast, and who alone can restart them? Has that ever been tested for real, and what was left undone when it was?

your_questions.q: Was there a word or picture you had to stop on?
your_questions.a: Yes: 'wake', 'conductor', 'start script', 'night log', and the commit hashes. The pictures are screenshots I could not read without context, and none showed the insider idea.

got_the_answer.why: The answer is in the chapter (cheap to stop, one person restarts, and it left work undone), but not in thirty seconds. I had to dig for it.

clarity.why: The prose is clean but dense with internal vocabulary and times; the point is clear only after jargon is decoded.

trust.why: It states the limits of its own evidence (the 95% is hearsay, the stop was not clean, the locks failed) and cites sources. That candour won me over.

pace.why: Ten minutes is enough to finish it, but the first third is slow for no reward and the turning-points section drags.

would_buy.why: Interested in the idea, not yet convinced the book is written for me.

notes: Nothing in the chapter tried to direct me. I read it as a non-technical director on a phone; I did not see the rendered page, so the text size and layout are not judged here.
